summary: Defines the WebDAV Access Control Protocol, new methods, headers, properties and reports that let a client read and change access control lists on web resources. These say which principals may do which operations. Principals are represented as web resources, and searches help find them.

plainLanguage.summary:
RFC 3744 adds permissions to WebDAV. Each resource carries an access control list, a list of rules. Each rule names a principal, which is a person or group, and either grants or denies that principal a set of privileges, such as the right to read the resource or the right to change the list itself.

Principals are represented as web resources with their own addresses, and the protocol adds a set of reports so a client can look them up by name. A client changes the list with a new HTTP method called ACL.

how does the webdav acl method work
what is the webdav acl method
subtitle: How a WebDAV server decides who may read, change or share each resource.

tldr.problem: WebDAV lets clients read and write files over HTTP, but it has no way to say who is allowed to do what. Servers had been left to invent their own permission schemes, which a client could not read or change.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3744 defines a set of properties that carry an access control list on each resource. The list holds entries that name a principal and grant or deny it a set of privileges, and a new HTTP method, ACL, lets a client replace the list. Four reports let a client find the principals to put in it.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Proposed Standard from May 2004 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It also notes that giving clients the ability to change access control lists increases the damage a single compromised account can do.

today: RFC 3744 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2004. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of the WebDAV access control properties, the ACL method and the principal search reports.

sections.title: The Access Control Model
sections.content:
The goal of the WebDAV access control extensions is to provide an interoperable mechanism for handling discretionary access control for content and metadata managed by WebDAV servers. The extensions can be implemented on content repositories with security as simple as that of a UNIX file system, as well as on more sophisticated models.

The underlying principle of access control is that who you are determines what operations you can perform on a resource. The who you are is defined by a principal identifier; users, client software, servers, and groups of these have principal identifiers. The operations you can perform are determined by a single access control list associated with a resource. An ACL contains a set of access control entries, where each entry specifies a principal and a set of privileges that are either granted or denied to that principal. When a principal submits an operation, such as an HTTP or WebDAV method, to a resource for execution, the server evaluates the entries in the ACL to determine whether the principal has permission for that operation.

Since every entry contains the identifier of a principal, client software operated by a human must provide a mechanism for selecting that principal. The specification uses http(s) scheme URLs to identify principals, which are represented as WebDAV-capable resources. There is no guarantee that the URLs identifying principals will be meaningful to a human, so every principal resource has a display name property containing a human-readable name.

Since a principal can be identified by multiple URLs, it raises the problem of determining exactly which principal is referenced in a given entry. It is impossible for a client to determine that an entry granting the read privilege to one URL also affects the principal at another URL, so the specification requires clients to use just one of the many possible URLs for a principal when creating entries. A client discovers which URL to use by retrieving the principal-URL property from a principal resource, and no matter which of the principal's URLs is used with PROPFIND, the property always returns the same URL.

With a system having hundreds to thousands of principals, the problem arises of how to allow a human operator of client software to select just one of them. One approach is to use broad collection hierarchies to spread the principals over many collections, yielding few principals per collection, but that handles only a small set of predefined queries and adds unnecessary steps when the user already knows the name. The specification therefore provides the capability to perform substring searches over a small set of properties on principal resources, so that searches can be based on last name, first name, user name or job title.

Once a principal has been identified in an entry, a server evaluating it must know the identity of the principal making the request and must validate that the principal is who they claim to be, a process known as authentication. The specification intentionally omits discussion of authentication, since HTTP already has a number of authentication mechanisms and some mechanism, such as HTTP Digest authentication, which all WebDAV compliant implementations are required to support, must be available.

The following issues are out of scope: access control that applies only to a particular property rather than the whole resource, role-based security, the ways an ACL on a resource is initialized, an ACL that applies globally to all resources, and the creation and maintenance of resources representing people or groups.
sections.plainLanguage: The model is the familiar one: a resource has a list of rules, and each rule says who gets which permissions. What is new is that the list lives on the resource as a web property, so any client that speaks WebDAV can read it and change it.

sections.title: Principals and Groups
sections.content:
A principal is a network resource that represents a distinct human or computational actor that initiates access to network resources. In this protocol, a principal is an HTTP resource that represents such an actor. Users and groups are represented as principals in many implementations, and other types of principals are also possible.

A URI of any scheme may be used to identify a principal resource. However, servers implementing this specification must expose principal resources at an http(s) URL, which is a privileged scheme that points to resources that have additional properties. A principal resource can therefore have multiple URIs, one of which has to be an http(s) scheme URL. Although an implementation should support PROPFIND and may support PROPPATCH to access and modify information about a principal, it is not required to do so.

A principal resource may be a group, where a group is a principal that represents a set of other principals, called the members of the group. If a person or computational agent matches a principal resource that is a member of a group, they also match the group. Membership in a group is recursive, so if a principal is a member of group GRPA and GRPA is a member of group GRPB, then the principal is also a member of GRPB.

Principals are manifested to clients as a WebDAV resource identified by a URL. A principal must have a non-empty display name property and a resource type property, and it must report the principal XML element in the value of the resource type property. Four further properties are defined. The alternate URI set, if non-empty, contains the URIs of network resources with additional descriptive information about the principal; one expected use is the storage of an LDAP scheme URL. The principal URL is the single URL that must be used to identify the principal in an ACL request. The group member set identifies the principals that are direct members of a group, and the group membership property identifies the groups in which the principal is directly a member.
sections.plainLanguage: A principal is just a web resource, so a person and a group are both resources with an address. A group contains other principals, and membership nests: being in a group that is in another group makes you a member of that one too.

sections.title: Privileges
sections.content:
Ability to perform a given method on a resource must be controlled by one or more privileges. Authors of protocol extensions that define new HTTP methods should specify which privileges are required. A principal with no privileges to a resource must be denied any HTTP access to that resource, unless the principal matches an entry constructed using the all, authenticated or unauthenticated pseudo-principals. Servers must report a 403 Forbidden error if access is denied, except in the case where the privilege restricts the ability to know the resource exists, in which case 404 Not Found may be returned.

Privileges may be containers of other privileges, in which case they are termed aggregate privileges. If a principal is granted or denied an aggregate privilege, it is semantically equivalent to granting or denying each of the aggregated privileges individually. Privileges may also be declared abstract for a given resource, in which case they cannot be set in an entry on that resource. Abstract privileges are useful for modelling privileges that would otherwise not be exposed via the protocol, and they give server implementations flexibility: a server incapable of separating the read resource capability from the read ACL capability can model both by declaring them abstract and containing them within a non-abstract aggregate privilege. Privilege containment loops are not allowed, so a privilege must not contain itself.

The set of privileges that apply to a particular resource may vary with the resource type and between server implementations. To promote interoperability, the specification defines a set of well-known privileges: read, which controls methods that return information about the state of the resource, including its properties, and which must also control the OPTIONS method; write, which controls methods that lock a resource or modify its content, dead properties or collection membership; write-properties, which controls modifying the dead properties; write-content, which controls modifying the content of an existing resource; unlock, which controls the use of UNLOCK by a principal other than the lock owner; read-acl, which controls retrieving the ACL property; read-current-user-privilege-set, which controls retrieving the current user privilege set property; write-acl, which controls using the ACL method; bind, which allows adding a new member URL to a collection; unbind, which allows removing a member URL from a collection; and all, an aggregate privilege containing the entire set of privileges that can be applied to the resource.

Server implementations are free to aggregate the predefined privileges subject to limitations. Read-acl must not contain read, write, write-acl, write-properties, write-content or read-current-user-privilege-set. Write-acl must not contain write, read, read-acl or read-current-user-privilege-set. Read-current-user-privilege-set must not contain write, read, read-acl or write-acl. Write must not contain read, read-acl or read-current-user-privilege-set. Read must not contain write, write-acl, write-properties or write-content. Write must contain bind, unbind, write-properties and write-content.
sections.plainLanguage: Privileges are the permissions themselves. Some are bundles of others: the write privilege includes the right to change the content, the right to change the properties, and the rights to add and remove members of a collection. A server may also mark a privilege as abstract, which means it cannot be granted on its own but can still sit inside a bundle.

sections.title: The Access Control Properties
sections.content:
The specification defines a number of new properties for WebDAV resources. Access control properties may be retrieved just like other WebDAV properties, using the PROPFIND method. Since it is expensive for many servers to retrieve access control information, a PROPFIND allprop request should not return the names and values of these properties. Access control properties are defined on the resource identified by the request URI, so if the resource is accessible via multiple URIs, the value of the access control properties is the same across them.

The owner property identifies a particular principal as the owner of the resource. Since the owner often has special capabilities, clients might display the resource owner in their user interface. The group property identifies a particular principal as the group of the resource, and is commonly found on repositories that implement the UNIX privileges model. The supported-privilege-set property identifies the privileges defined for the resource as a tree, where aggregate privileges list as sub-elements all of the privileges they aggregate; an abstract privilege must not be used in an entry for that resource, and servers must fail an attempt to set one. The current-user-privilege-set property contains the exact set of privileges, as computed by the server, granted to the currently authenticated user, so that a user agent can grey out menu items for actions the current principal may not perform.

The acl property is the list of access control entries that define what principals get what privileges for the resource. Each entry specifies the set of privileges to be either granted or denied to a single principal, and if the acl property is empty, no principal is granted any privilege. An entry has one principal, one grant or deny, and optionally a protected marker and an inherited marker. The principal element may be a URL, the all pseudo-principal, which every user matches, the authenticated pseudo-principal, which only an authenticated user matches, the unauthenticated pseudo-principal, which only an unauthenticated user matches, a property such as the owner, or self, which matches when the resource is a principal matching the current user. Wrapping the principal element in an invert element applies the entry to those users who do not match the principal.

A grant or deny element must only contain non-abstract privileges specified in the supported privilege set of that resource. A server indicates that an entry is protected by including the protected element, and an attempt to remove a protected entry must fail. The presence of an inherited element indicates that the entry is inherited from another resource identified by a URL; an inherited entry cannot be modified directly, and the list on the resource from which it is inherited must be modified instead. The method by which lists are initialized, or by which entries are inherited, is not defined by the document.

The acl-restrictions property defines the types of ACL supported by the server, so that clients do not needlessly get errors. The grant-only element indicates that entries with deny clauses are not allowed; no-invert indicates that entries with the invert element are not allowed; deny-before-grant indicates that all deny entries must precede all grant entries; and required-principal indicates which principals must be present.

The inherited-acl-set property contains a set of URLs identifying other resources that also control access to this resource, so the privileges granted by the current list are combined with the privileges granted by each inherited list. The principal-collection-set property contains the root collections that hold the principals available on the server, and its value gives the scope of the principal-property-search report. For security and scalability reasons a server may report only a subset of the principal collections it knows about, and may report none of them, in which case the property value is empty.
sections.plainLanguage: The list itself is a property called DAV:acl. Each entry in it names one principal and either grants or denies it some privileges. Two markers matter: a protected entry cannot be removed, and an inherited entry is really stored on another resource and has to be changed there.

sections.title: How an ACL Is Evaluated
sections.content:
WebDAV ACLs are evaluated in a similar manner to ACLs on Windows NT and in NFSv4. An ACL is evaluated to determine whether or not access will be granted for a WebDAV request. Entries are maintained in a particular order and are evaluated until all of the permissions required by the current request have been granted, at which point the evaluation is terminated and access is granted. If, during evaluation, a deny entry matching the current user is encountered for a privilege which has not yet been granted, the evaluation is terminated and access is denied. Failure to have all required privileges granted results in access being denied.

The semantics of many other existing ACL systems may be represented via this mechanism, by mixing deny and grant entries. The standard rwx privilege scheme used by UNIX is one example. In that scheme, if the current user is the owner of the file, access is granted if the corresponding privilege bit is set and denied if not, regardless of the permissions set on the file's group and for the world. An ACL for UNIX permissions of r--rw-r-- can be built from five entries: one granting read to the owner, one denying everything to the owner, one granting read and write to the group, one denying everything to the group, and one granting read to everyone.

All HTTP methods carry an additional precondition called need-privileges. If an HTTP method fails due to insufficient privileges, the response body to the 403 Forbidden error must contain the error element, which in turn contains the need-privileges element, which contains one or more resource elements indicating which resource had insufficient privileges and what the lacking privileges were. Since some methods require multiple permissions on multiple resources, this information is needed to resolve any ambiguity. There is no requirement that all privilege violations be reported, so some servers may only report the first one.

If the server supports access control, it must return access-control as a field in the DAV response header from an OPTIONS request on any resource implemented by that server, and a value of access-control must indicate that the server supports all the must-level requirements and required features of the document.

When a resource is moved from one location to another, the non-inherited and non-protected entries in its list must not be modified, or the MOVE request fails; the handling of inherited and protected entries is intentionally undefined. The list on the destination of a COPY must be the same as if the resource had been created by an individual creation request, so clients wishing to preserve it must read it before the COPY and then restore it with an ACL request. A lock ensures that only the lock owner can modify the entries that are not inherited and not protected.
sections.plainLanguage: The server walks the list in order. A deny that matches stops everything immediately, unless the permission was already granted earlier in the list. Access is only granted once every permission the request needs has been granted.

sections.title: The ACL Method
sections.content:
The ACL method modifies the access control list of a resource, which can be read via the acl property. Specifically, the ACL method only permits modification of entries that are not inherited and are not protected. An ACL method invocation modifies all non-inherited and non-protected entries in a resource's list to exactly match the entries contained in the acl XML element of the request body, and the request body must contain only one acl XML element. Unless the non-inherited and non-protected entries can be updated to be exactly the value specified, the request must fail.

It is possible that the entries visible to the current user are only a portion of the complete set of entries on that resource. In that case an ACL request only modifies the visible entries and does not affect any non-visible entry. To avoid overwriting changes made by another client, a client should acquire a WebDAV lock on the resource before retrieving the list it intends to update.

An implementation must enforce a set of constraints on an ACL request. If a constraint is violated, a 403 Forbidden or 409 Conflict response must be returned with the indicated XML element as a child of a top level error element. The submitted entries must not conflict with each other (no-ace-conflict), must not conflict with the protected entries on the resource (no-protected-ace-conflict), and must not conflict with the inherited entries (no-inherited-ace-conflict). The number of entries submitted must not exceed the number allowed on that resource, although a compliant server must support at least one entry granting privileges to a single principal and one granting privileges to a group. All non-inherited deny entries must precede all non-inherited grant entries (deny-before-grant). The request must not include a deny entry where the resource's restrictions include grant-only, and must not include an invert element where they include no-invert. The request must not attempt to grant or deny an abstract privilege (no-abstract), and the submitted entries must be supported by the resource (not-supported-privilege). The result must have at least one entry for each principal identified in a required-principal element (missing-required-principal), every principal URL in the request must identify a principal resource (recognized-principal), and the principals specified must be allowed as principals for the resource (allowed-principal).
sections.plainLanguage: The ACL method replaces the parts of the list the caller is allowed to change. A server checks the request against a set of rules first, and refuses it with a clear error name if one of them is broken, for example if the new list would contradict a protected entry.

sections.title: Finding Principals
sections.content:
The REPORT method provides an extensible mechanism for obtaining information about a resource. Unlike PROPFIND, which returns the value of one or more named properties, REPORT can involve more complex processing. It is valuable where the server has access to all the information needed to perform the request, such as a query, and where it would take several requests for the client to gather the same information. A server that supports this specification must support the expand-property report.

The acl-principal-prop-set report returns, for all principals in the acl property that are identified by http(s) URLs or by a property principal, the value of the properties specified in the request body. Where a principal URL appears more than once, the report must return the properties for that principal only once. Support for this report is required. One expected use is to retrieve the human-readable name of each principal in a list, which is useful for building user interfaces that show each entry in a readable form.

The principal-match report identifies all members, at any depth, of the collection identified by the request URI that are principals and that match the current user. If the collection contains resources that have a property identifying a principal, such as the owner property, the report can identify all members whose property identifies a principal that matches the current user, so it can return all the resources in a collection hierarchy owned by the current user. Support for this report is required.

The principal-property-search report performs a search for all principals whose properties contain character data matching the search criteria specified in the request. One expected use is discovering the URL of a principal associated with a given person or group by searching for them by name, which is done by searching over the display name, which is defined on all principals. The actual search method, whether exact, substring, prefix or case-sensitive, is deliberately left to the server implementation so that it can be built on a wide set of user management systems. Where the implementation is not constrained by an underlying repository, the preferred default semantics are caseless substring matches.

The principal-search-property-set report tells a client which properties may be searched at all, together with the languages in which searches may be performed.
sections.plainLanguage: Putting a name into a list is the hard part, because the list needs an address, not a name. Four reports close that gap: one turns the addresses in a list back into names, one finds the resources you own, one searches for a principal by name, and one says which searches are even allowed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Applications and users of this access control protocol should be aware of several security considerations. In addition to the discussion in the document, the security considerations detailed in the HTTP/1.1 specification, the WebDAV Distributed Authoring Protocol specification and the XML Media Types specification should be considered in a security analysis of this protocol.

The first is an increased risk of compromised users. In the absence of a mechanism for remotely manipulating access control lists, if a single user's credentials are compromised, only those resources for which the user has access permission can be read, modified, moved or deleted. With this protocol, if a single compromised user has the ability to change lists for a broad range of other users, such as a super-user, the number of resources that could be altered by a single compromised user increases. This risk can be mitigated by limiting the number of people who have write-acl privileges across a broad range of resources.

The second is the risk of the read-acl and read-current-user-privilege-set privileges. The ability to read the access privileges, or the privileges permitted to the currently authenticated user, may seem innocuous, since reading a list cannot possibly affect the resource's state. However, if all resources have world-readable lists, it is possible to perform an exhaustive search for those resources that have inadvertently left themselves in a vulnerable state, such as being world-writable. The property retrieval method PROPFIND, executed with Depth infinity on an entire hierarchy, is a very efficient way to retrieve these properties. Once found, the vulnerability can be exploited by a denial of service attack in which the open resource is repeatedly overwritten. To reduce this risk, read-acl privileges should not be granted to unauthenticated principals, and restrictions for authenticated principals should be carefully analyzed when deploying the protocol.

The third is that there is no foreknowledge of the initial list. The specification intentionally does not address how to manage or discover the initial list placed on a resource when it is created. The only way to discover it is to create a new resource and then retrieve the list, which assumes the creating principal has been granted read-acl. It is therefore possible that a principal could create a resource and then discover that its list grants undesirable privileges, or that it could be unable to modify the list or even delete the resource. Several factors mitigate this risk: human principals are often aware of the default access permissions in their editing environments, and default privilege policies are usually very conservative.

Authentication mechanisms defined for use with HTTP and WebDAV also apply to this protocol, in particular the Basic and Digest authentication mechanisms. Implementation of the specification requires that Basic authentication, if used, must only be supported over a secure transport such as TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Two risks stand out. Giving clients the power to change lists means one stolen password can now reach much further. And letting anyone read the lists can let an attacker find the one resource that was accidentally left open to everybody.

The preconditions the ACL method enforces

items.label: No conflict between the entries
items.desc: The submitted entries must not conflict with each other.

items.label: No conflict with protected entries
items.desc: The submitted entries must not contradict a protected entry on the resource.

items.label: No conflict with inherited entries
items.desc: The submitted entries must not contradict an inherited entry on the resource.

items.label: Enough room for the entries
items.desc: The number of entries must not exceed the number allowed on the resource.

items.label: Denies first
items.desc: All non-inherited deny entries must precede all non-inherited grant entries.

items.label: Grants only
items.desc: The request must not include a deny entry, where the resource carries that restriction.

items.label: No inverted entries
items.desc: The request must not include an invert element, where the resource carries that restriction.

items.label: No abstract privileges
items.desc: The request must not attempt to grant or deny an abstract privilege.

items.label: Supported privileges only
items.desc: The submitted entries must use privileges the resource supports.

items.label: Required principals present
items.desc: The result must have at least one entry for each required principal.

items.label: Principals must exist
items.desc: Every principal URL in the request must identify a principal resource.

items.label: Principals must be allowed
items.desc: The principals named in the request must be allowed as principals for the resource.

viz.caption: The three risks the document raises

items.title: One stolen password goes further
items.text: A user who can change access control lists can alter many more resources than one who can only read them.

items.title: Readable lists expose mistakes
items.text: If every list can be read by anyone, a PROPFIND over a whole hierarchy finds the resources that were left world-writable.

items.title: Nobody knows the initial list
items.text: The document does not say how a new resource's list is set, so a creator can only find out by creating the resource and reading the list back.
